newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Redland profits reel,but sees rebound.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Redland profits reel,but sees rebound.

text.p: British building materials group Redland Plc was the latest in the sector to report reeling profits on Thursday due to bad weather and weak markets, but it saw a second half pickup as Germany recovers and costs are cut.
Even so, chief executive Robert Napier warned that despite expectations of a better second half, full-year figures would not fully recover from a very poor first quarter.
That quarter was largely responsible for first half profits plunging to 95.0 million pounds ($148 million) from 165.2 million. Turnover fell to 1.18 billion from 1.29 billion.
The dividend was frozen at 5.5 pence as expected and earnings per share collapsed to 6.8 pence from 14.3 pence.

Trading in the second half kicked off in line with 1995. But Napier offered a note of caution. "We will have a better second half than last year due to cost savings, but it will not make up for the first quarter." For the full year, he added "The damage will be slightly recovered."
The second half optimism was built on two main factors: The first was expected cost savings.
Napier said the benefit in the second part of the financial year would be 15 to 20 million pounds, but he added this would be partly offset by factors like redundancy costs.
But in 1997 the savings would give a full benefit of 25 to 30 million for the year, he said.
The second factor fuelling recovery was an improved German market, which accounted for the biggest chunk of group profits and sales.
Redland's optimism was in marked contrast to RMC Group last week, whose doom-laden German outlook prompted a shareprice slump.
But Napier explained "We see it differently from RMC. We're very focused on the housing and re-roofing market and housing has picked up."

He said the West German market was improving, with East Germany also ahead. But he said the East German business would be adversely affected by the removal of a layer of tax breaks relating to the region from 1997.
"It will lead to a slowdown next year in new housing in East Germany," agreed Napier. "But this will be outweighed by gains in the West German market."
Redland shares had a roller-coaster ride after the results. At first shares tumbled nine pence to 435.5p because the profits were at the lower end of forecasts.
But as the market digested evidence of a second half upturn, shares had bounced to 454.5p, a rise of 10 pence.
One marketmaker said: "The headline figure looked alarming but the company's statement points to a recovery in the second half and that's what the market is focusing on."
